papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How do different mechanisms interact in the decision-making of LLMs? The paper proposes to trace how one mechanism becomes dominant in the final prediction.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formulates the competition of mechanisms and traces how mechanisms compete within LLMs, identifying critical components and attention positions that control the strength of mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates how to trace the competition of mechanisms in LLMs and reveals insights into how factual and counterfactual mechanisms interact and can be controlled.
papers.key_findings:
In early layers, the factual attribute is encoded in the subject position, while the counterfactual is in the attribute position.
The attention blocks write most of the factual and counterfactual information to the last position.
All the highly activated heads attend to the attribute position regardless of the specific type of information they promote. The factual information flows by penalizing the counterfactual attribute rather than promoting the factual one.
We can up-weight the value of a few very localized values of the attention head matrix to strengthen factual mechanisms substantially.
Similar tokens confuse the model more easily, and larger models suffer more from such confusion.
papers.limitation: Logit inspection can occasionally fail to reflect the actual importance of vocabulary items, especially in the early layers of the network.
future_direction: Extend the competition of mechanisms formulation to more complex mechanisms and multi-step reasoning.
Explore other mechanisms and their competitions in future work.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research aims to bridge the gap between empirical success and our scientific understanding of the inner workings of large language models (LLMs). However, most existing research focuses on analyzing a single mechanism, such as how models copy or recall factual knowledge. In this work, we propose a formulation of competition of mechanisms, which focuses on the interplay of multiple mechanisms instead of individual mechanisms and traces how one of them becomes dominant in the final prediction. We uncover how and where mechanisms compete within LLMs using two interpretability methods: logit inspection and attention modification. Our findings show traces of the mechanisms and their competition across various model components and reveal attention positions that effectively control the strength of certain mechanisms. Code: https://github.com/francescortu/comp-mech. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/francescortu/comp-mech.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: BACH-V: Bridging Abstract and Concrete Human-Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) genuinely understand abstract concepts, or merely manipulate them as statistical patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an abstraction-grounding framework to show that LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstract concepts and concrete decisions, enabling value-driven control.
papers.conclusion: These findings indicate LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstraction and action, providing a mechanistic and operational foundation for building value-driven autonomous AI systems with more transparent, generalizable alignment and control.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on abstract value descriptions generalize to concrete events and decisions, demonstrating cross-level transfer.
Steering value representations causally shifts concrete judgments and decisions but leaves abstract interpretations unchanged, indicating stable abstract value anchors.
LLMs maintain distinguishable internal representations for different value concepts across abstraction levels (A-A, A-C, C-C).
Intermediate layers are most effective for encoding abstract value representations.
The asymmetry in steering effects suggests abstract values function as stable anchors rather than malleable activations.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) genuinely understand abstract concepts, or merely manipulate them as statistical patterns? We introduce an abstraction-grounding framework that decomposes conceptual understanding into three capacities: interpretation of abstract concepts (Abstract-Abstract, A-A), grounding of abstractions in concrete events (Abstract-Concrete, A-C), and application of abstract principles to regulate concrete decisions (Concrete-Concrete, C-C). Using human values as a testbed - given their semantic richness and centrality to alignment - we employ probing (detecting value traces in internal activations) and steering (modifying representations to shift behavior). Across six open-source LLMs and ten value dimensions, probing shows that diagnostic probes trained solely on abstract value descriptions reliably detect the same values in concrete event narratives and decision reasoning, demonstrating cross-level transfer. Steering reveals an asymmetry: intervening on value representations causally shifts concrete judgments and decisions (A-C, C-C), yet leaves abstract interpretations unchanged (A-A), suggesting that encoded abstract values function as stable anchors rather than malleable activations. These findings indicate LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstraction and action, providing a mechanistic and operational foundation for building value-driven autonomous AI systems with more transparent, generalizable alignment and control.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Disentangling Deception and Hallucination Failures in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs by separating knowledge existence from behavior expression?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs, and constructs a controlled environment for analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Representational separability analysis shows that knowledge existence is a dominant signal in distinguishing failure modes.
Sparse autoencoder reveals feature groupings associated with different behavioral cases, indicating a global split driven by knowledge existence.
Activation steering can induce bidirectional transitions between correct and deceptive behaviors, demonstrating causal control over behavior expression.
Hallucination cases are not reversible via activation steering, highlighting the distinction between knowledge absence and suppression.
Deception involves suppression of knowledge expression rather than knowledge removal, as verified through jailbreak probing.
papers.abstract: Failures in large language models (LLMs) are often analyzed from a behavioral perspective, where incorrect outputs in factual question answering are commonly associated with missing knowledge. In this work, focusing on entity-based factual queries, we suggest that such a view may conflate different failure mechanisms, and propose an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression. Under this formulation, hallucination and deception correspond to two qualitatively different failure modes that may appear similar at the output level but differ in their underlying mechanisms. To study this distinction, we construct a controlled environment for entity-centric factual questions in which knowledge is preserved while behavioral expression is selectively altered, enabling systematic analysis of four behavioral cases. We analyze these failure modes through representation separability, sparse interpretability, and inference-time activation steering.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: LLM world models are mental: Output layer evidence of brittle world model use in LLM mechanical reasoning
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal 'world models,' or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities learned from data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs show some ability to reason about mechanical systems (pulley systems) using heuristics like pulley counting and can differentiate functional from jumbled systems, but their internal representations are brittle and fail when the task requires understanding of nuanced structural connectivity, indicating limited world model use.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer mixed support for the view that LLMs reason over world models independently from output token probabilities. The brittleness of these representations, especially in Study 3, aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.key_findings:
In Study 1, LLMs performed above chance in estimating mechanical advantage (MA) and their estimates correlated with ground truth MA, but they relied on a pulley-counting heuristic and selectively attended to relevant features.
LLMs could distinguish functional from non-functional (jumbled) pulley systems with high accuracy (F1=0.8) in Study 2.
In Study 3, LLMs failed to differentiate functional from non-functional (but connected) pulley systems, performing at chance level (F1=0.46).
The results suggest LLMs have some latent knowledge of pulley systems but lack robust internal models for nuanced structural reasoning.
The brittleness of these representations aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty regarding whether tested pulley stimuli are truly out-of-distribution; exposure during training cannot be ruled out.
Difficulty deconfounding output layer token representations from potential latent world models represented in network weights without combining with interpretability research.
future_direction: Future work should further deconfound pulley count from MA and employ novel or synthetic diagramming languages to limit reliance on familiar formats like TikZ.
Extending the paradigm to other physical systems (e.g., levers, gear trains) may help assess the breadth of these internal representations.
Integrating the present approach with interpretability research may help elucidate the network circuits underlying reasoning over world models.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal world models, or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities? We adapt cognitive science methodologies from human mental models research to test LLMs on pulley system problems using TikZ-rendered stimuli. Study 1 examines whether LLMs can estimate mechanical advantage (MA). State-of-the-art models performed marginally but significantly above chance, and their estimates correlated significantly with ground-truth MA. Significant correlations between number of pulleys and model estimates suggest that models employed a pulley counting heuristic, without necessarily simulating pulley systems to derive precise values. Study 2 tested this by probing whether LLMs represent global features crucial to MA estimation. Models evaluated a functionally connected pulley system against a fake system with randomly placed components. Without explicit cues, models identified the functional system as having greater MA with F1=0.8, suggesting LLMs could represent systems well enough to differentiate jumbled from functional systems. Study 3 built on this by asking LLMs to compare functional systems with matched systems which were connected up but which transferred no force to the weight; LLMs identified the functional system with F1=0.46, suggesting random guessing. Insofar as they may generalize, these findings are compatible with the notion that LLMs manipulate internal world models, sufficient to exploit statistical associations between pulley count and MA (Study 1), and to approximately represent system components' spatial relations (Study 2). However, they may lack the facility to reason over nuanced structural connectivity (Study 3). We conclude by advocating the utility of cognitive scientific methods to evaluate the world-modeling capacities of artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Toward universal steering and monitoring of AI models
papers.research_question: How can we extract linear representations of concepts from internal activations of AI models to enable steering and monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a scalable method using Recursive Feature Machines (RFM) to extract linear concept representations from internal model activations, enabling effective steering and monitoring across diverse models and concepts.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the power of using internal representations for steering and monitoring AI models, providing a cost-efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The RFM method can extract concept vectors that enable steering and monitoring in LLMs, VLMs, and reasoning models.
Concept vectors are transferable across languages and can be combined for multi-concept steering.
Newer, larger models are more steerable, and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting.
Concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content) and outperform judge models.
The method is scalable, requiring under one minute and fewer than 500 training samples on a single GPU.
papers.abstract: Modern AI models contain much of human knowledge, yet understanding of their internal representation of this knowledge remains elusive. Characterizing the structure and properties of this representation will lead to improvements in model capabilities and development of effective safeguards. Building on recent advances in feature learning, we develop an effective, scalable approach for extracting linear representations of general concepts in large-scale AI models (language models, vision-language models, and reasoning models). We show how these representations enable model steering, through which we expose vulnerabilities, mitigate misaligned behaviors, and improve model capabilities. Additionally, we demonstrate that concept representations are remarkably transferable across human languages and combinable to enable multi-concept steering. Through quantitative analysis across hundreds of concepts, we find that newer, larger models are more steerable and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting. We show how concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content). We demonstrate that predictive models built using concept representations are more accurate for monitoring misaligned content than using models that judge outputs directly. Together, our results illustrate the power of using internal representations to map the knowledge in AI models, advance AI safety, and improve model capabilities.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs: An Exploration Using Cognitive Dual-System Theory
papers.research_question: How can the contributions of knowledge retrieval and reasoning adjustment be separated and quantified in large language models during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cognition attribution framework based on dual-system theory to decouple knowledge and reasoning in LLMs, revealing domain-specific reasoning benefits, scaling effects, and a hierarchical separation of knowledge (lower layers) and reasoning (higher layers).
papers.conclusion: The proposed cognition attribution architecture offers a novel perspective for understanding LLM cognition and provides insights into scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and the reasoning limitations of small models.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, chemistry) and potentially impairing knowledge-intensive domains.
Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Scaling also makes reasoning significantly more prudent (reduces overthinking) and modestly more intelligent (increases correction) in specific domains.
Knowledge retrieval primarily occurs in lower network layers, while reasoning adjustments are localized in higher layers, suggesting a functional separation.
Small LLMs tend to overthink more than they correct during reasoning, leading to negative or limited reasoning gains.
LLMs exhibit a human-like anchoring effect, which reasoning adjustment helps to mitigate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA; future work should extend to open-ended generation.
The study does not include ultra-large models (>100B parameters).
The methods are simplified and may not fully capture the underlying mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to open-ended generation tasks.
Include ultra-large models (>100B parameters) in the study.
Conduct a more in-depth exploration of the phenomena observed using the framework.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) leverage both knowledge and reasoning during inference, the capacity to distinguish between them plays a pivotal role in model analysis, interpretability, and development. Inspired by dual-system cognitive theory, we propose a cognition attribution framework to decouple the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. In particular, the cognition of LLMs is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary phases: knowledge retrieval (Phase 1) and reasoning adjustment (Phase 2). To separate these phases, LLMs are prompted to generate answers under two different cognitive modes, fast thinking and slow thinking, respectively. The performance under different cognitive modes is analyzed to quantify the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. This architecture is employed to 15 LLMs across 3 datasets. Results reveal: (1) reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, and chemistry) and potentially imparing knowledge-intensive domains. (2) Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Additionally, parameter scaling make LLMs reasoning significantly more prudent, while moderately more intelligent. (3) Knowledge primarily resides in lower network layers, while reasoning operates in higher layers. Our framework not only helps understand LLMs from a "decoupling" perspective, but also provides new insights into existing research, including scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and limitations of small-model reasoning.

papers.title: Explaining Cognitive Phenomena with Internal Representations: A Mechanistic Perspective
papers.research_question: What criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that representational explanations in cognitive science are a species of mechanistic explanation, and defines representational mechanisms as those that meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
papers.conclusion: Representational mechanisms are those that use decouplable, action-guiding, error-detection-affording structural representations, and a mechanistic explanation of a cognitive phenomenon is representational if it postulates such a mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanation, answering how-questions about cognitive capacities.
A representational mechanism is one that has at least one component part whose function is to represent something, and such a component must meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
The proposed account integrates correspondence and action-guidance approaches to representation, aiming to provide a robust notion that meets the 'job description challenge'.
Examples from cognitive science, such as emulation theory and predictive coding, can be seen as meeting the proposed conditions for representational mechanisms.
The account provides criteria for determining when a mechanistic explanation is genuinely representational, which is a step towards resolving the debate between representationalism and antirepresentationalism.
papers.limitation:
The proposed account might be too restrictive, potentially rendering many existing cognitive-scientific theories nonrepresentational.
The proposal is a general, incomplete, and highly idealized functional sketch that abstracts away from structural details.
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the fact that the notion of internal representation has - at least according to some - a fundamental role to play in the sciences of the mind, not only has its explanatory utility been under attack for a while now, but it also remains unclear what criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation in the first place. The aim of this article is to propose a solution to this latter problem. I will assume that representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanations and proceed by proposing a general sketch of a functional architecture of a representational cognitive mechanism. According to the view on offer here, representational mechanisms are mechanisms that meet four conditions: the structural resemblance condition, the action-guidance condition, the decouplability condition, and the error-detection condition.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their Chain-of-Thought?
papers.research_question: How robust are reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controlled benchmark to evaluate the robustness of reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought, finding that models are generally robust but with trade-offs in efficiency and style invariance.
papers.conclusion: The findings clarify how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity under disruptions, reveal trade-offs between robustness and compute cost, and point to training targets for improving recovery strategies.
papers.key_findings:
RLLMs are generally robust to interventions, with robustness improving with model size.
Robustness degrades when interventions occur early in the chain-of-thought.
Paraphrasing interventions suppress doubt-like expressions and reduce performance.
Doubt expressions play a central role in recovery from perturbations.
Neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by over 200%, while paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy.
future_direction: preserving appropriate doubt
improving style robustness
developing recovery strategies that control token cost
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) generate step-by-step chains of thought (CoTs) before giving an answer, which improves performance on complex tasks and makes reasoning more transparent. But how robust are these reasoning traces to disruptions that occur within them? To address this question, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that perturbs a model's own CoT at fixed timesteps. We design seven interventions (benign, neutral, and adversarial) and apply them to multiple open-weight RLLMs across Math, Science, and Logic tasks. Our results show that RLLMs are generally robust, reliably recovering from diverse perturbations, with robustness improving with model size and degrading when interventions occur early. However, robustness is not style-invariant: paraphrasing suppresses doubt-like expressions and reduces performance, while other interventions trigger doubt and support recovery. Recovery also carries a cost: neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by more than 200%, whereas paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy. These findings provide new evidence on how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity, identify doubt as a central recovery mechanism, and highlight trade-offs between robustness and efficiency that future training methods should address.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.
